questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the inferior oblique muscle?

options.label: C
options.text: It originates from the annulus of Zinn

options.label: D
options.text: It is supplied by the third cranial nerve

questions.answerText: It originates from the annulus of Zinn
questions.solutionHtml:
It originates from the annulus of Zinn
  • ANNULUS OF ZINN ( TENDINOUS RING )
  • TENDINOUS RING gives origin to all the rectus muscles and levator palpebrae superioris(LPS).
  1. Superior Rectus originates from the superior part of the common tendinous ring.
  2. Inferior Rectus originates from the inferior part of the common tendinous ring.
  3. Medial Rectus originates from the medial part of the common tendinous ring.
  4. Lateral Rectus originates from the lateral part of the common tendinous ring


Parson’s Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 416

questions.stem: The best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with 15-degree accommodative esotropia of recent onset is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Refractive correction
  • Accommodative esotropia, or refractive esotropia, is one of the most common forms of esotropia (crossed eye), which is a type of strabismus, or eye misalignment. It refers to eye crossing that is caused by the focusing efforts of the eyes as they try to see clearly. Patients with refractive esotropia are typically farsighted (hyperopic). This means that the eyes must work harder to see clearly, particularly when the object of regard is up close.
  • Initial treatment for accommodative esotropia usually involves the prescription of eyeglasses or contact lenses to correct the patient’s refractive error (hyperopia). By letting the eyeglasses do the work, the eyes can relax their focusing or accommodative effort. In turn, this will reduce the convergence or crossing stimulus and the eyes will straighten as they relax. Glasses or contacts which are used to treat accommodative esotropia should be worn full time


Parsons Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 434

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man came to the OPD because he had suddenly developed double vision. On examination, it was found that his right eye, when at rest, was turned medially. The most likely anatomical structures involved are:

options.label: A
options.text: Medial rectus and superior division of the oculomotor nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Inferior oblique and inferior division of oculomotor nerve

questions.solutionHtml:
Lateral rectus and abducens nerve
  • The lateral rectus muscle is a muscle on the lateral side of the eyeball in orbit. It is one of six extraocular muscles that control the movements of the eye.
  • The lateral rectus muscle is responsible for the lateral movement of the eyeball, specifically abduction. Abduction describes the movement of the eye away from the midline (i.e. nose), allowing the eyeball to move horizontally in the lateral direction, bringing the pupil away from the midline of the body
  •  It is the only muscle supplied by the abducens nerve, cranial nerve VI. The abducens nerve exits the brainstem from the pons-medullary junction and travels through the superior orbital fissure to innervate the lateral rectus muscle. The lateral rectus muscle is innervated through the tectospinal tract



Parson’s Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 408

questions.stem: Which muscle is inserted closest to the limbus of the eye?
questions.solutionHtml:
Medial Rectus
  • Recti muscles are not inserted equidistant from the limbus and don't form a circle concentric with the limbus. Thus these muscles form a spiral (the spiral of tillaux).
  • The medial rectus and inferior rectus are inserted 5mm and 6.5mm from the limbus.
  • The lateral rectus and superior rectus are inserted 6.9mm and 7.7mm from the limbus respectively.
  • Thus medial rectus is inserted closest to the limbus and the superior rectus farthest from the limbus.




Parson’s Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 355-362

questions.stem: Which two muscles constitute the superior transverse ligament of Whitnall?
questions.solutionHtml:
Levator palpebrae superioris & superior oblique
  • The superior transverse ligament of the eye (also known as Whitnall's ligament) is a transverse ligament surrounding the levator palpebrae superioris muscle close to its partial implantation into the skin of the upper eyelid. The muscle also attaches to the superior tarsal plate and into the orbital bone.
  • It is a thickened band of orbital fascia extending from the trochlear pulley to the lacrimal gland & its fossa.
  • It is formed by condensation of the superior sheaths of the levator muscle joined medially by the sheath of the reflected tendon of the superior oblique muscle. It forms a true check ligament of the levator muscle.



Parson’s Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 27

questions.stem: Which of these muscles form ligaments of Lockwood?
questions.solutionHtml:
All of the above

It's a thickened sling of fascial sheath extending from the posterior lacrimal crest to the lateral orbital tubercle, on which rests the eyeball. It is formed by a fusion of expansions from the muscular sheaths of the medial rectus, inferior oblique, inferior rectus & lateral rectus muscles joined with the thickened inferior part of the tenon’s capsule.



Parsons Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 355

questions.stemHtml: The green-coloured structure derives its nerve supply from which the nucleus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Superior Colliculus
  • The muscle marked is the superior rectus. The superior rectus is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, the nucleus of which is situated at the level of the superior colliculus.
  • The nuclear complex from which the oculomotor nerve arises consists of:
    • Several groups of large motor neurons collectively called the oculomotor nucleus Smaller preganglionic parasympathetic neurons called the Edinger-Westphal preganglionic nucleus
    • The motor neuron groups of the oculomotor nucleus innervate, in dorsoventral order, the ipsilateral inferior rectus, inferior oblique, and medial rectus. A medially placed column of cells innervates the contralateral superior rectus




Comprehensive Ophthalmology by A K Khurana, 7th EditionPage No. 354

questions.stem: Rotatory movement along the anteroposterior axis in which the superior pole of the cornea moves laterally is called as?
questions.solutionHtml:
Excycloduction
  • Excycloduction (extorsion). It is a rotatory movement along the anteroposterior axis in which the superior pole of the cornea (12 O'clock point) moves laterally (external rotation).
  • The movements possible for the eyeball are elevation, depression, adduction, abduction, intorsion, and extorsion. These movements occur along three axes, i.e., transverse, vertical, and anteroposterior.
  1. Movement around the vertical axis of the eye in one eye is referred to as adduction and abduction.
  2. Movement around the horizontal axis of the eye in one eye is referred to as elevation and depression.
  3. Movement around the anteroposterior axis will be defined as intorsion and extorsion.




Parsons Disease of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page No. 355

questions.stem: The yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus in dextroversion is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Left Medial Rectus

The yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus in dextroversion is the left medial rectus.




Comprehensive Ophthalmology by A K Khurana, 7th EditionPage No. 338

questions.stem: Rajesh was posted in the ophthalmology department. The Head of the Department asks him to check the range of extraocular movements. How many cardinal fields are there?
questions.solutionHtml:
6
  • There are six cardinal positions (fields) of gaze. These are the positions that allow examination of each of the twelve extraocular muscles. They are as follows:
  • Dextroversion (right lateral rectus and left medial rectus)
  • Levoversion (left lateral rectus and right medial rectus)
  • Dextroelevation (right superior rectus and left inferior oblique)
  • Levo Elevation (left superior rectus and right inferior oblique)
  • Dextro Depression (right inferior rectus and left superior oblique)
  • Levo Depression (left inferior rectus and right superior oblique)



Comprehensive Ophthalmology by A K Khurana, 7th EditionPage No. 353

questions.stem: A surgeon decides to relocate one or more extraocular muscles for squint surgery. Which of the following is the most common palsy surgeon can see?
questions.solutionHtml:
6th nerve palsy
  • Transposition refers to the relocation of one or more extraocular muscles to substitute for the action of an absent or severely deficient muscle. The most common indication is severe lateral rectus weakness due to acquired palsy of the 6th cranial nerve palsy.
  • Isolated muscle paralysis Lateral rectus and superior oblique are the most common muscles to be paralysed singly, as they have separate nerve supplies. Isolated paralysis of the remaining four muscles is less common, except in congenital lesions.
  • In paralysis of the right lateral rectus muscle there occurs :
  • Overaction of the left medial rectus,
  • Contracture of the right medial rectus and
  • Inhibitional palsy of the left lateral rectus muscle.



Comprehensive Ophthalmology by A K Khurana, 7th EditionPage No. 369
